I think inflation lost and we’re seeing it reflected today in the price of energy. I think the fever has broken in the energy trade. title: Why ExxonMobil and Chevron Reminded Investors to Keep it Simple - MarketBeat
content:
Some of 2026's best large-cap stories didn't come from Silicon Valley. They came from Texas. At the market close on Nov. 3, Chevron Corp. NYSE: CVX was up more than 46% over the past year. ExxonMobil NYSE: XOM has had an even more impressive run, up nearly 56%. Both stocks also pay dividends that keep growing. Chevron yields about 3% and has raised its payout for 38 straight years. ExxonMobil's streak of annual dividend increases now stands at 42 years with a yield of around 2.3%. Yet many investors spent the year looking elsewhere. Capital chased artificial intelligence (AI) and the technology names tied to it. Energy stocks were treated as a trade on oil prices rather than on the businesses themselves. The trade seemed simple: when crude cools off, so will these stocks. Third-quarter results, released by Chevron and ExxonMobil on Oct. 30, challenge that view. Higher prices helped. But refining strength, cost discipline and balance sheet repair did much of the work. Both companies also absorbed accounting headwinds that should reverse. That sets up a case for further upside, even after a big year. Chevron reported adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. That's up from $1.85 per share a year ago. Brent crude averaged $97 per barrel versus $69, lifting upstream results. But the bigger swing came from refining. Downstream earnings jumped to $4.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. Chevron's U.S. refineries processed a record 1.09 million barrels per day. Crude unit utilization reached nearly 98%. That matters because refining profits depend on margins, not just crude prices. Strong margins offset a 109,000 barrel-per-day drop in international production. Chevron tied that decline to price-driven entitlement effects and the Middle East conflict. Cash flow tells the rest of the story. Chevron generated $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow. It paid $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion of stock. It still cut total debt by $3.5 billion. Net debt fell $7.8 billion in the quarter alone. Management also laid out a growth path. Chevron's Venezuelan joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over five years. The company says that could more than double production there. In the Bakken, new agreements should cut midstream costs by roughly 50%. Both moves aim to improve returns per barrel, not just add volume. ExxonMobil posted adjusted earnings of $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share. That compares with $3.52 per share in the second quarter. GAAP earnings came in at $3.72 per share. Operating cash flow totaled $25.7 billion, and free cash flow reached $19.1 billion. Like Chevron, ExxonMobil leaned on refining. Adjusted Energy Products earnings more than doubled from the prior quarter to $9.1 billion. Its U.S. Gulf Coast refineries ran at 100% crude unit utilization. Meanwhile, upstream earnings fell on lower prices and a Guyana entitlement impact. The integrated model did exactly what it was built to do. CEO Darren Woods made a point investors should note. He described the gains as lasting improvements, not just the product of favorable pricing. ExxonMobil estimates its structural cost savings at $16.9 billion since 2019. Lower costs reduce the oil price needed to keep earnings and dividends growing. Shareholders are getting paid along the way. ExxonMobil returned $9.4 billion in the quarter, including $5.1 billion in buybacks. It plans $20 billion in repurchases for 2027. It also declared a $1.07 quarterly dividend. Net debt has fallen by nearly $11 billion so far this year. Both reports carried a detail that's easy to miss. Rising oil prices created "timing effects" that reduced reported earnings. These come mainly from marking derivatives to market before physical barrels are delivered. Chevron absorbed $1.58 billion in negative timing effects. ExxonMobil's hit totaled roughly $2.5 billion. ExxonMobil notes these impacts are expected to unwind in later periods. In other words, part of the third quarter's profit was deferred, not lost. If prices stabilize, that reversal could boost results in the coming quarters. It's a potential catalyst many investors may not be watching. None of this makes these stocks completely safe. Future results still depend heavily on commodity prices and refining margins. Both are elevated partly because of the Middle East conflict. If supply disruptions ease, margins could compress quickly. Chevron's total production also slipped from a year ago, which bears watching. Valuation is less forgiving after a 50% run. Investors buying now are paying for continued strength. That makes execution over the next few quarters more important, not less. The lesson from this quarter isn't complicated. Two of the world's largest energy companies are generating enormous amounts of cash. They're cutting debt, buying back stock, and raising dividends. And they're doing it with growing help from refining and cost cuts, not just oil prices. Investors who chased complexity this year may have overlooked that simplicity. For those still on the sidelines, the latest results suggest the story isn't finished. Patient, income-focused investors may find that keeping it simple still pays. Excluding working-capital movements, cash flow declined roughly 15.7%, suggesting cash timing explains only part of the sequential slowdown. Strong annual profit growth deserves attention, but so does the softer quarterly cash performance. title: Shell Agrees to $1.45 Billion Sale of North West Shelf Stake - The Globe and Mail
content: Shell plcSHEL, through subsidiary Shell Australia Pty Ltd, has agreed to sell its 16.67% non-operated interest in Australia’s North West Shelf (“NWS”) project to subsidiaries of XRG P.J.S.C. The transaction carries a base consideration of $1.45 billion, subject to customary adjustments, along with an additional payment tied to specified milestones. Announced on Nov. 3, 2026, the agreement has an effective date of Jan. 1, 2026, and is expected to close in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. The effective date is distinct from the anticipated closing date, which remains dependent on these conditions being met. The divestment is part of Shell’s effort to streamline its portfolio and focus investment on advantaged integrated gas positions. For investors, it shows the company monetizing a mature asset while maintaining its broader commitment to natural gas and liquefied natural gas (“LNG”). Shell’s 16.67% holding is a minority, non-operated interest: it gives the company a share in the project without responsibility for day-to-day operations. The $1.45 billion base consideration will be subject to customary adjustments and could be supplemented by the milestone-linked payment. The buyers will also assume decommissioning obligations and provide security for them. Decommissioning covers the eventual closure or removal of facilities when they are no longer needed. Transferring these responsibilities may reduce Shell’s future exposure to retirement costs, although the benefit depends on the final terms and completion of the deal. The NWS project is an integrated LNG and domestic gas development in Western Australia, involving interconnected joint ventures with Woodside, ChevronCVX, BPBP, Shell, MIMI and CNOOC. Shell’s interest includes upstream assets, pipeline and midstream infrastructure, project companies, offtake arrangements and related petroleum and pipeline interests. Production from NWS’ original gas fields has declined, leaving spare capacity at the Karratha Gas Plant, which processes gas for domestic supply and LNG exports. The project is moving toward a mix of its own resource production and third-party toll processing. Under this model, other producers can pay to use the facility to process their gas, changing the project’s operating and commercial profile. As production from the original fields eases, future plant utilization will increasingly depend on attracting third-party gas volumes and securing toll-processing arrangements. The sale follows Shell’s 2023 divestment from the Browse project, a proposed offshore development intended to send gas to Karratha for processing and export through NWS infrastructure. Together, the transactions indicate a more selective approach to Shell’s Australian gas portfolio, not a complete exit from the country. XRG, an international energy investment company focused on natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions, is adding an established Australian gas position to its broader portfolio through the proposed acquisition. Shell retains a substantial Australian presence through its operated QGC project and Prelude floating LNG facility, the Crux development, and joint venture interests in Arrow Energy and Gorgon. These positions preserve its exposure to Australian gas production, LNG supply and infrastructure after the NWS sale. Globally, Shell expects to grow LNG sales by 4-5% annually through 2030. The NWS divestment is therefore a portfolio reallocation: Shell is reducing its stake in one mature project while continuing to invest in other gas and LNG assets. The company has not indicated a change to its long-term LNG growth target. The milestone-linked payment could add to the base consideration, but it is contingent and should not be treated as guaranteed. The expected 2027 closing remains subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions, so investors should monitor progress and any changes to the timetable. Investors should watch how Shell deploys the proceeds and whether its remaining Australian projects support the group’s LNG plans. The sale also involves a trade-off: after completion, Shell will no longer participate in NWS production or any upside from higher third-party processing volumes. The final financial contribution will depend on completion, customary adjustments and any contingent payment. The transfer of decommissioning responsibilities also changes Shell’s future obligations tied to the asset. Overall, the North West Shelf sale demonstrates Shell’s focus on portfolio quality and disciplined capital allocation. The deal provides a $1.45 billion base value and reduces the company’s exposure to a mature, non-operated project, while Shell retains several important Australian gas and LNG assets. The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though? Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Chevron (CVX). Chevron currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.59, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 29 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.59 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 29 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 20 are Strong Buy and three are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 69% and 10.3% of all recommendations. Check price target & stock forecast for Chevron here>>> The ABR suggests buying Chevron, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation. Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation. In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures. The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5. It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements. In addition, the different Zacks Rank grades are applied proportionately to all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide current-year earnings estimates. In other words, this tool always maintains a balance among its five ranks. Another key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank is freshness. The ABR is not necessarily up-to-date when you look at it. But, since brokerage analysts keep revising their earnings estimates to account for a company's changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in indicating future price movements. title: Chevron Advances Iraq Oilfield Deal, Expands Growth Prospects - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX is moving closer to expanding its footprint in Iraq, potentially strengthening its international production opportunities and long-term growth prospects. Iraq's Ministry of Oil announced that it had reached an agreement with Chevron on key provisions of the development contract for the West Qurna 2 oil field. The progress sets the stage for a formal agreement by the end of 2026, according to Iraqi News, The development represents an important step in Chevron's efforts to establish a stronger presence in Iraq's oil industry. Alongside West Qurna 2, the company is exploring opportunities involving the Nasiriyah oil field and four additional exploration blocks, potentially creating a broader platform for future investment. The latest progress followed a meeting between Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair and Chevron's vice president of business development, Joe Cook, on Nov. 3. Discussions focused on the West Qurna 2 oil field and opportunities to deepen cooperation between the two parties. Although significant portions of the development contract have been agreed upon, the final agreement remains pending. Both sides are targeting completion and formal signing by the end of 2026, providing a potential timeline for Chevron's expanded involvement in the project. West Qurna 2 represents a strategically important opportunity for Chevron, given Iraq's substantial hydrocarbon resources and the potential to expand international production. Greater involvement in the country's oilfields could strengthen the company's upstream portfolio and provide additional opportunities to deploy its technical capabilities. However, the project's contribution to Chevron's production and earnings will depend on the final contractual terms, investment requirements, development schedule and operational execution. Additional Opportunities Could Expand Chevron's Iraq Presence Chevron's discussions with Iraq extend beyond West Qurna 2. The two sides have agreed to continue negotiations regarding the Nasiriyah oil field and four additional exploration blocks. These potential agreements could broaden Chevron's exposure to Iraq's upstream sector, creating opportunities to participate in multiple development and exploration projects. A larger portfolio in the country could also provide greater flexibility in allocating capital across assets with different development timelines. For Chevron, international projects remain an important component of its long-term growth strategy. The company can potentially leverage its experience in complex oilfield development, reservoir management and production technology to support operations in Iraq. Nevertheless, exploration opportunities typically involve geological uncertainty, substantial upfront investment and longer development periods. Their financial benefits may not materialize immediately, making the eventual project terms and investment commitments important considerations for investors. Iraq's renewed engagement with Chevron comes as the government attempts to attract additional foreign investment and strengthen its energy infrastructure. Over the past six months, the country has increased cooperation with U.S. and other international energy companies to improve production capabilities, modernize facilities and address operational challenges. The Iraqi government has also expressed willingness to support Chevron and other American energy companies by reducing investment obstacles and facilitating greater participation in the oil and gas sector. Khudair highlighted the importance of American expertise in oilfield development, technology transfer and workforce training. These priorities could give Chevron opportunities to contribute beyond production growth, particularly through operational improvements and developing local technical capabilities. For Iraq, stronger partnerships with international operators could help improve the efficiency of its oil industry and support its efforts to overcome infrastructure and export-related constraints. Iraq's efforts to attract international energy investment are taking place amid significant challenges in oil transportation. Interruptions to shipments associated with the Strait of Hormuz blockade have increased pressure on the country's energy sector, highlighting the importance of maintaining reliable export channels and strengthening production infrastructure. Although Chevron's West Qurna 2 agreement does not directly resolve Iraq's export challenges, the potential development underscores the country's determination to sustain investment in its oil industry despite operational uncertainties. For Chevron, developments in Iraq could offer additional international growth opportunities, although geopolitical risks, contractual uncertainty and transportation disruptions remain important factors to monitor. What Does the Iraq Deal Mean for Chevron Investors? The progress on West Qurna 2 is a potentially favorable development for Chevron, particularly from a long-term strategic perspective. The agreement could establish a foundation for expanded upstream operations in Iraq while opening additional opportunities through Nasiriyah and other exploration blocks. However, investors should distinguish between progress toward a contractual agreement and actual production or earnings growth. The formal signing, project economics, capital commitments and development milestones will determine the financial significance of Chevron's expanded involvement. The next important developments will include the finalization of the West Qurna 2 contract, progress on the additional projects and clarity regarding investment and production plans. Overall, Chevron's advancing negotiations with Iraq reinforce its international growth ambitions. If the agreements translate into economically attractive development opportunities, the country could become a more meaningful contributor to Chevron's long-term upstream portfolio.  stepped into the market spotlight as the energy major reported a third-quarter scorecard marked by record production, a reading that topped market expectations and extended a string of strong quarterly prints. The headline draw was volume, with barrels flowing at the fastest pace in the company's history after the landmark absorption of Hess assets began feeding the portfolio. Market watchers scrutinized the production tally, the cash figures and the early read on how the sizeable acquisition was knitting into the wider business. The report arrived during the thick of the reporting calendar, when several of the largest American energy names crossed the wire within days of one another. Crude prices had traded through a choppy stretch, so the market leaned on volume growth and cost control to gauge how the company was faring. The company cast the quarter as evidence that the enlarged asset base was already lifting output and cash generation, a message that framed how the stock traded once the numbers landed. The defining thread of the quarter was the integration of Hess, a transformational combination that closed after a long and closely followed arbitration process. Folding those assets into the fold handed the company a prized stake in the prolific Guyana offshore basin, alongside Bakken shale acreage and other positions. The quarter offered the market its clearest look yet at how the enlarged company performs with the new barrels fully in the mix, and the early signals pointed to meaningful volume gains. Integration of a deal this size is rarely seamless, and the company acknowledged near-term frictions tied to accounting, synergy capture and the mechanics of merging two large organizations. Even so, the company stressed that the combination was tracking ahead of its own internal markers on cost savings and volume contribution. The Guyana stake in particular gives the firm a growth engine with low supply costs, a feature that stood out sharply in a quarter where the crude benchmark offered little tailwind. Through the Hess combination, the company now carries a sizeable interest in the Stabroek block offshore Guyana, one of the most consequential crude discoveries of the past decade. The basin has scaled rapidly from first oil to a meaningful supplier, and each new floating production vessel has added fresh capacity on a brisk cadence. For the company, the stake transforms the growth arithmetic, layering a low-cost offshore engine on top of its existing upstream base. Guyana's appeal lies in its economics. The barrels come out of the ground at a cost that stays competitive even when prices soften, and the development pipeline stretches well into the next decade. The quarter's commentary leaned on this asset as a durable source of volume and cash, and the company framed it as one of the clearest reasons the sizeable acquisition was worth the long legal fight that preceded the close. Alongside the new Guyana exposure, the Permian Basin remained a bedrock of the production mix. Output across the West Texas and New Mexico shale fields kept flowing steadily, supported by efficiency gains, tighter well design and a disciplined development cadence. The company has long described the Permian as a free-cash engine, and the quarter reinforced that framing, with the basin contributing a reliable stream of barrels that require modest fresh capital to sustain. The broader upstream base spans continents, from the deepwater of the American Gulf to projects in Kazakhstan, Australia and West Africa. That geographic spread gives the company a buffer against any single region's swings, and the company underscored how the enlarged portfolio blends mature cash generators with fresh growth barrels. title: ExxonMobil Stock Trades at a Premium: Is It Still Worth Buying? - The Globe and Mail

West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is trading at more than $98 per barrel. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration in its latest short-term energy outlook projected WTI at $88.21 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, similar to BP and Chevron. Image Source: The U.S. Energy Information Administration The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. On its third-quarter 2026 call, the integrated major mentioned that in the prolific basin it is now operating three automated drilling rigs, and planning to increase the count to 25% of the total fleet in the basin next year. By 2028, ExxonMobil is planning to boost the proportion to 50%, to further lower its cost structures amid technological advancements. Considering its downstream business, ExxonMobil's investments in upgrading its U.S. refineries should help the company produce more high-value fuels, particularly diesel. By making better use of existing facilities, XOM can expand output without the high costs of building new refineries. These improvements are expected to support stronger profit margins and cash flow over the long term. Moreover, XOM has a strong balance sheet, on which it could rely when the business environment turns unfavorable. During the September quarter of this year, the company lowered its debt by more than $9 billion. Considering the price chart, ExxonMobil has jumped 57.6% over the past year, outpacing the industry’s 57.3% growth. BP and Chevron have gained 36.3% and 48.8%, respectively, over the same period. title: Chevron Earnings Call Highlights Cash, Growth and Resilience - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron ((CVX)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call. Chevron’s Earnings Call Signals Strong Momentum Despite Market Risks Chevron’s earnings call carried a strongly positive tone, led by robust cash generation, a stronger balance sheet, steady production and record refining and natural gas output. Management also highlighted AI gains and broad growth opportunities, although lower sequential earnings, volatile commodity prices, permitting issues and a future non-cash accounting loss remain notable risks. Chevron reported third-quarter earnings of $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. Cash flow from operations excluding working capital was $16.6 billion, and adjusted free cash flow totaled $14.2 billion. Chevron reduced debt by more than $3 billion and increased cash by more than $4 billion during the quarter. Net debt to cash flow from operations improved to 0.4 times, giving the company greater financial flexibility. Third-quarter production was nearly 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day despite entitlement impacts and planned maintenance turnarounds. U.S. upstream output stayed above 2 million barrels per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Chevron posted record quarterly natural gas production of more than 9 billion cubic feet per day, led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean. Its U.S. Gulf of America operations also set a new quarterly deepwater production record. Permian production remained above 1 million barrels per day for a sixth straight quarter. Capital spending per barrel improved by more than 25%, while drilling and completion spending fell 40% and facility spending declined 50%. Chevron expanded its acreage and secured new fiscal terms in Venezuela, making the business more competitive and immediately accretive to free cash flow. The company plans to double production from its three joint ventures to about 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, with total costs below $20 per barrel. Chevron is on track to reach roughly 300,000 barrels per day of gross Venezuelan production by year-end, up 20% in 12 months. It markets all crude from the three ventures, with most volumes shipped to U.S. refineries. A planned 50% reduction in Bakken midstream tariffs should improve returns, expand economic inventory and increase operating flexibility. Chevron plans to reduce its rig count from three to two while sustaining about 180,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The Hess Midstream restructuring is expected to increase corporate return on capital employed by 0.5% and deconsolidate $3.7 billion of debt. Chevron also expects recurring earnings and an immediate improvement in Bakken upstream earnings and cash flow after the transaction. Chevron achieved record crude throughput across its refining system and record quarterly U.S. crude throughput. More than 80% of U.S. refinery turnarounds over the past two years were completed with first-quartile duration, supporting reliability. A proprietary catalyst at Chevron’s largest U.S. refineries lifted distillate production by 10% after changes to cut points. Third-quarter distillate yield at those refineries reached 46%, while Pascagoula recorded its strongest diesel production in at least three or four years. Chevron accelerated debottlenecking at Pasadena, adding about 15% of refinery capacity at nominal cost. The company also plans to increase Pascagoula capacity by another 7% by 2030. Upstream debottlenecking projects added more than 85,000 barrels per day of capacity. TCO’s third-generation plant gained 20% of capacity, Ballymore rose 7%, and Anchor increased capacity by 33%, or 25,000 barrels per day. Chevron added 22 million acres over the past two years, doubling its exploration footprint across 12 new basins. In the latest quarter, it added six Gulf of America blocks as well as acreage in Angola, Nigeria, Guinea-Bissau and Egypt. The company made 15 infrastructure-led discoveries over two years with a 40% success rate, above the industry average. AI pattern recognition found more than 150 leads in the Gulf of America, with 16 prospects advancing to evaluation and 30 net new prospects identified. Chevron said AI generated more than $100 million of value capture year to date in 2026. In the DJ Basin, the technology cut loss-production events by 50%, while AI-enabled production optimization is now deployed in the Permian, Bakken and PZ assets. Chevron’s ApEx system uses four petabytes of data and a century of company knowledge to assemble basin information in hours rather than months. ScoutAI can build basin assessments in hours instead of weeks and is now deployed in 10 new basins. Advanced Chemicals increased cumulative oil-equivalent production in the Permian by as much as 23% during the first 12 months. Chevron is also testing next-generation chemistry through field pilots to improve recovery further. Predictive maintenance, centralized data and AI-supported decisions helped keep Australian LNG reliability strong. Gorgon and Wheatstone operated above nameplate capacity, and the combined assets delivered record third-quarter production. Chevron reaffirmed its framework of consistent dividend growth, efficient investment, a strong balance sheet and share repurchases through the cycle. The company has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years and plans to keep annual buybacks in the $2.5 billion-to-$3 billion range. Organic capital expenditures totaled $3.9 billion in the quarter. Fourth-quarter spending is expected to rise in line with seasonal trends, but full-year capital expenditures are still expected to finish at the low end of annual guidance. Project Kilby is a 2.67-gigawatt, behind-the-meter power project in West Texas backed by a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. Chevron is targeting a final investment decision, first power in 2028 and full energization in 2031, with potential expansion to combined-cycle power. Chevron said terms in Iraq currently appear more attractive than they have historically and that it is working with the ministry on a development plan. The company is also discussing similar opportunities with several Middle Eastern governments, building a pipeline of growth options beyond 2030. A significant share of Chevron’s fleet is owned or covered by long-term charters agreed before the conflict, at pre-conflict rates. Controlled transportation and greater use of equity crude, which has reached about 50% at times at certain refineries, are supporting current results. Adjusted third-quarter earnings were $1.6 billion below the prior quarter. The decline shows that strong operating performance did not fully offset a less favorable pricing and timing environment. Adjusted upstream earnings fell because of lower realizations, reduced liftings and unfavorable timing effects. Lower depreciation, depletion and amortization expenses and tax benefits partly offset those pressures. Working capital was negatively affected by sharp commodity price increases late in the quarter. Management said rising prices can create additional timing effects, while those impacts generally unwind when prices fall. When the Hess Midstream transaction closes, Chevron expects a one-time non-cash after-tax loss of $3 billion to $4 billion. Management emphasized that the charge reflects deconsolidation accounting rather than the underlying economics of the deal. Management cited a $64 intra-quarter price spread, with crude prices ranging from $68 to $132 per barrel during the quarter. Chevron said the volatility has not changed its short-term capital allocation approach. Chevron expects refining margins to eventually moderate as refinery runs recover and exports increase.  returned to the spotlight after the energy major reported record oil output and credited much of the surge to its acquisition of Hess, a deal that closed earlier in the year and has quickly begun feeding fresh barrels into the production mix. The update topped expectations across the market and reignited commentary about how fast the megadeal is paying off. As one of the largest integrated energy companies in the world, Chevron tends to move sector sentiment whenever it reports, and this update carried extra weight because it offered the first clear look at how the Hess assets are contributing. Traders parsed the figures for evidence that the combination is delivering the volumes and cash flow the company promised when it pursued the tie-up. Renewed interest also reflects the price backdrop. With crude soft and under pressure, the market has leaned harder on which majors can keep expanding output while keeping spending in check. Chevron used its update to argue that the Hess barrels, together with its own growth engines, position it to keep volumes climbing even through a weaker price stretch. The defining event behind the update was the Hess acquisition, a long-pursued combination that handed Chevron a prized stake in the prolific offshore fields of Guyana alongside additional acreage in the United States. After a drawn-out path to completion, the deal has moved from headline to hard numbers, and the latest quarter showcased its early contribution to volumes. Management framed the integration as running ahead of schedule, pointing to barrels from the acquired assets flowing into the production total and to cost savings beginning to surface. That messaging matters because the market had watched the lengthy arbitration and regulatory journey closely, and signs of a smooth handover help ease lingering questions about the price paid. The Guyana stake in particular has drawn attention as one of the fastest-growing sources of new supply anywhere, and Chevron now shares in that ramp through its enlarged footprint. Framed this way, the deal reads as a reshaping of the company's growth profile rather than a one-off addition, giving it a longer runway of low-cost barrels to draw on. The quarterly report showed production reaching fresh highs even as the price of crude eased from earlier levels, and the headline earnings came in ahead of what the market had penciled in. The company leaned on rising volumes and firm operating performance to offset the drag from softer commodity prices. Reporting periods for the majors tend to be closely parsed because earnings swing with crude, and the market looks for signs that a company can sustain cash flow through weaker stretches. Chevron pointed to its enlarged production base and disciplined spending as the levers helping it keep delivering regardless of where oil trades on any given day. The timing added to the interest, arriving while the broad market reflected in the S&P 500 stayed fixated on technology earnings and heavy spending on data-center power. That left energy names to trade largely on their own merits, and a record-output beat from a major of this size stood out against an otherwise tech-dominated backdrop. The oil and gas space has spent recent sessions pulled in several directions at once. Crude has been soft and under pressure, while natural gas and liquefied natural gas themes have stayed active and electricity demand tied to data centers has lent support to power-linked names. An integrated major such as Chevron sits across many of these crosscurrents at once. Softer crude has sharpened the focus on cost discipline and volume growth, since operators that can keep expanding cheap barrels are better placed to weather a weaker price environment. That dynamic has put a premium on scale, low breakeven costs and a deep pipeline of projects, all areas the company highlights when presenting its direction. Sentiment across the group has also been shaped by the steady climb in global energy demand and the push to balance conventional output with lower-carbon ventures. Each shift in those conditions tends to move the whole sector rather than any single name, keeping the broader conversation lively and the majors firmly in view. Chevron operates across the full energy value chain, spanning upstream exploration and production, refining and a chemicals arm run through a long-standing joint venture. That integrated structure gives the company a footprint that stretches across many countries and lets different segments offset one another as commodity prices move through their cycles. The upstream business centers on finding and producing crude oil and natural gas, and it has become the engine of the company's growth story thanks to the Permian Basin, offshore Guyana and a mix of global projects. Downstream, a network of refineries turns those barrels into fuels and lubricants, adding a layer that can cushion the group when crude softens. This breadth is often framed as a source of resilience. When crude prices ease, refining can help steady the overall picture, and when oil firms, the upstream arm carries the momentum. That balance has long defined how the market reads the company and helps explain why its updates draw such close attention. The scale of the operation also gives Chevron a reach that few rivals can match, from deepwater developments to sprawling refining complexes. title: Chevron rides a diesel crunch to its biggest ever refining profit - TradingView
content: Chevron CVX reported record refining profit of $4.93 billion for the third quarter, more than triple the $1.1 billion a year earlier. A global diesel shortage helped. Bloomberg reported that attacks tied to wars in Iran and Ukraine have knocked out up to 10% of worldwide refining capacity. Chevron ran its U.S. refineries at 98% capacity and processed a record 1.09 million barrels of crude oil a day. Net income rose nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share. Adjusted earnings of $5.28 per share beat the $4.87 analysts expected, and revenue of $67.8 billion topped the $61.6 billion forecast. Profit from oil and gas production climbed about 70% to $5.7 billion. Chevron limited buybacks to $2.5 billion and used extra cash to pay down $3.5 billion of debt. The company expects to pump 300,000 barrels a day in Venezuela by year-end. Chevron shares rose about 2% in premarket trading Friday. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services.
